dek_candidates: What the DRHP discloses about A B Infrabuild Limited's business, offer, financials and risks — sourced to the filing, page by page.
A Mumbai infrastructure contractor that earns more than half its revenue from government clients is bringing a 44.28-lakh-share issue to the SME Board. Here is what its DRHP says.

beats.beat: A contractor does not invent work; it responds to tenders. The DRHP describes the cycle: a client floats a tender, the contractor bids, the lowest quote wins a Letter of Acceptance, a performance guarantee is deposited, and only then does site work begin. Revenue therefore follows a pipeline of bids, not a recurring order stream.

The product list is plain in the filing: designing and building railway platforms, station buildings, gauge conversion and track laying; bridges of many types — beam, cantilever, arch, suspension, cable-stayed, truss; and bituminous and concrete roads. The second segment is a ready-mix concrete plant at Kashimira, Thane.

The client list is dominated by public bodies: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation, Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority, Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation, plus a few private names. Western Railway has been a client since 2006.

Concentration is the defining business fact: Western Railway contributes 52% of the orders on hand, and the key customers as a group gave the company 57% of revenue in FY2018. One client relationship, not a broad book, drives this company.

Geography is also narrow: the DRHP calls itself a major player in Mumbai infrastructure, slowly consolidating in Maharashtra. It uses the 'box pushing' technique in projects and says its strength is experienced professionals with more than 20 years in the industry.
The company's own SWOT lists the flip side: slow pace of government projects, working-capital crunch, and changes in government policies.

business.heading: What the company does
business.purpose: Explain how an infrastructure contractor actually operates — the tender-to-handover process — then name the concrete products, customers, and the dependence that defines the business.

beats.beat: Revenue has fallen for three straight years. Restated revenue from operations was ₹90.21 crore in FY2015, ₹74.53 crore in FY2016, ₹73.44 crore in FY2017 and ₹60.53 crore in FY2018. The business is roughly a third smaller in four years.

Profit tells a very different curve. Net profit after adjustments was ₹0.78 crore in FY2015, ₹0.33 crore in FY2016, a near-zero ₹0.16 crore in FY2017, and then jumped to ₹3.15 crore in FY2018 — a spike worth questioning given the revenue decline.

Profit before interest, depreciation and tax — a proxy for operating cash earnings — was ₹7.84 crore in FY2014, ₹9.46 crore in FY2015, ₹7.83 crore in FY2016, ₹6.76 crore in FY2017 and ₹9.29 crore in FY2018. The FY2018 jump is visible here too.

The balance sheet is dominated by short-term borrowings, which rose from ₹30.82 crore in FY2014 to ₹35.37 crore in FY2018. Long-term borrowings came down from ₹5.87 crore to ₹1.33 crore over the same period. Total assets grew from ₹70.62 crore to ₹82.32 crore.
The DRHP itself flags that the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years and that short-term debt is heavy. That matters for an issuer raising money largely to fund working capital.

The filing's own price-basis table adds two FY2018 reference numbers: an EPS figure of ₹12.59 and a Return on Net Worth of 28.14%, with earlier years far lower. These are inputs for the valuation section below, not a recommendation.

financials.heading: Financials: shrinking revenue, a profit spike, and heavy short-term debt
financials.purpose: Tell the five-year restated financial story in plain terms — revenue, profit, cash earnings, debt, assets — with actual figures converted to ₹ crore, then point to what the trend implies.

beats.beat: Control is concentrated in one man. Amit Bholanath Mishra is the promoter and holds 74,95,476 equity shares, or 90.949% of the pre-issue paid-up capital. He is also the Managing Director.

Outside the promoter, the next-largest holder is Hatim Sakerwala, a key management person, with 9% of equity shares. The other whole-time directors — Bharat Kumar Parmar, Shree Prakash Singh and Mukesh Pandey — each hold 300 shares.
The management team is young: CFO Anchal Pachori is 28 and a chartered accountant; Company Secretary Mohit Soni is 26 and an associate member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India.

Governance flags in the filing: related-party transactions exist — FY2018 loans taken from KMP/board members of ₹68.4 lakh, director remuneration of ₹57.7 lakh, and ₹324.3 lakh of outstanding related-party payables. The company also says litigation involving the company, promoter and directors is pending, the promoter has not been declared a willful defaulter, and no criminal cases have been filed against the directors.

Two other red flags belong in this section: two companies promoted by the promoter were struck off by the Registrar of Companies in March 2016 for non-operation, and the company had issued equity shares in the previous 12 months at a price that may be lower than the coming issue price. The DRHP also discloses there is no independent project-appraisal agency and no monitoring agency for fund deployment.

governance.heading: Control, management and governance flags
governance.purpose: Show who controls the company, how founder-heavy the shareholding is, who manages it, and what governance blemishes the filing discloses.

beats.beat: The industry is infrastructure and construction — power, bridges, dams, roads, urban infrastructure — which the filing says is a highly fragmented, working-capital-intensive market contributing roughly 8% of India's GDP at constant prices.

The DRHP's demand story is macro: rising urbanization and disposable income, government flagship programs including Smart Cities, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All, eased FDI norms in 15 sectors including real estate and construction, and a stated requirement of ₹50 trillion in infrastructure investment by 2022.

The filing quotes supporting macro numbers: India's eight core industries grew 4.2% in 2017-18, GDP was projected to grow above 7% in 2017, logistics was expected to grow at a 10.5% CAGR from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020, and FDI in construction development from April 2000 to December 2017 stood at US$24.67 billion.

Competition is described only in kind, not by name: the DRHP says the industry has competitors in both the organized and unorganized sectors. No named peer companies appear in the extracted filing pages.
The headwinds the company itself acknowledges in its SWOT are slow government projects, working-capital pressure, and policy changes — the same three risks that show up in its financials.

industry.heading: The market it operates in
industry.purpose: Give the reader the industry setting — size, scale, demand drivers, and the specific headwinds the filing itself names — without pretending the DRHP is a market study.

beats.beat: A B Infrabuild is a Mumbai-based infrastructure company with two businesses: it builds civil infrastructure — rail, bridges, roads — and it runs a ready-mix concrete plant. It makes money the way most contractors do: by winning tenders, largely from government clients.

The issue is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, but the issue price is yet to be determined. The DRHP says the money will go mainly toward working capital — ₹1,130 lakh — plus general corporate purposes.

The single fact that frames this filing: Indian Railways is the company's largest customer, with the top clients together contributing 57% of revenue in FY2018 and Western Railway alone making up 52% of orders on hand. Keep that in mind through every section that follows.

offer.heading: The offer and what the money is for
offer.purpose: Lay out the mechanics of this specific issue — size, price, intermediaries, and objects — while flagging what the DRHP leaves undecided or undisclosed.

beats.beat: One-client concentration: Indian Railways is the largest customer at 57% of FY2018 revenue, and Western Railway alone is 52% of orders on hand. The DRHP says losing this relationship would cause a significant dip in revenue.

Dependence on winning government tenders: revenue depends on bids being accepted, and projects are awarded to the lowest quote. If bids fail or margins are squeezed to win, financial condition suffers — a risk the DRHP states directly.

Liquidity pressure: the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years, carries heavy short-term borrowings, and had ₹405.02 lakh of unsecured loans repayable on demand as of March 31, 2018. A repayment demand or a working-capital crunch could hurt cash flow and profitability.

The order book is not a guarantee: contracts in the order book may be adjusted, cancelled or suspended by clients, and cost overruns can reduce profits or cause losses. The filing says the order book is not necessarily indicative of future revenue.

Governance and process risks: two promoter companies were struck off by the ROC, no independent agency appraised the proposed project, no monitoring agency oversees fund deployment, and shares were issued in the prior 12 months at a price that may be below the issue price.

risks.heading: The material risks, stated specifically

beats.beat: The DRHP's basis-for-issue-price section on page 54 is the intended valuation anchor: it lists historical EPS and RoNW for FY2016 to FY2018. The FY2018 column shows EPS of ₹12.59 and RoNW of 28.14%; the issue price itself is still ₹[●].

A comparison-of-accounting-ratios table exists on page 55, and the DRHP says the issue price will be justified by those ratios. But the extracted digest does not include the names of the peer companies or the individual P/E, EPS, NAV and RoNW figures in that table.

Because the peer names and multiples are missing from the extract, this report cannot — and will not — build the requested peer comparison table or compute an implied price range. That is a limitation of the available excerpt, not a conclusion about the price.
